title: Scam victim issues warning after losing $750,000 of life savings | A Current Affair

asr.full_text: Hello I'm Sylvia Jeffries, welcome to A Current Affair. We're constantly told to be on the lookout for scams but sometimes they're incredibly hard to pick. Tonight, how to spot the red flags on fake investments that are robbing Aussies of their life savings. Once again, this is a classic identifier that they are very sophisticated. They are willing to go that extra mile even if it takes them a few months to get one hit that one hit is a very large sum. so they must qualify they are very sophisticated They're willing to go that extra mile Even if it takes them a few months for that one hit that one hit is a very large sum I've learnt that there's nothing you should do online without physically checking I feel like I've been responsible for trying to sort my life out now It has just put me back in the biggest hole Michelle Lowery thought she was investing in government and bankbonds when she lost $750,000 of her life savings. You know, I was just starting to move forward after the death of my husband. And this is just, yeah, it put me right back there, stress-wise, anxiety, everything. It's just myself and I've got my three kids and, you know, this money was going to help us have our lifestyle together, you know, build ourselves back together and that's been taken away from me now. Michelle was looking online for term deposits when she came across a website for EQR Securities. I checked out that they were a registered company with ASIC, and they had an Australian Financial Securities license number. I gave the information to my accountant, as well, and for him to verify the legitimacy of- of the purchase of the bonds, and the company. So in December last year, she went to her local bank and teletransferred her money to an account provider. I had communication then saying that EQR Securities, which is the company that were buying the bonds on my behalf, received the funds and that I could log in to a portal and find my receipts online. I logged in once and then, after that, I couldn't seem to get in. I kept asking Will Hughes, which was the name of the man at EQR Securities I was dealing with. Will Hughes is a name we've heard before. Jody Bridges, who we interviewed in May, lost $5,300 in a similar scale, of our securities I was dealing with. Will Hughes is a name we've heard before. Jody Bridges, who we interviewed in May, lost $500,000 in a similar scam, and was also duped by a man called Will Hughes who had a British accent. The money is your fully, fully safe, okay? If there was something untoward, I wouldn't even bother calling you back. Jody, you're money is absolutely fine and it is being recalled. I tried to ring him and said, well, what's going on? It's now May. The coupons were supposed to go in in April and then all of a sudden EQR Securities didn't have a phone number, he couldn't be contacted and I went onto the internet to get onto their website and everything had been taken down. 75-year-old Sorosh Calopeze was looking to invest in bonds when he lost US$100,000 after entering his details on a fake bond comparison website called Savings Connection. Called me and said that he was from NAB and he was going to be an account manager because there is a limit on my bank. So the first amount I transferred was $59.74 or something as a trial run. And my bank did let it go through. And then the next day, I deposited 100,000. And that time, CBA called me early in the morning at around eight o'clock and said that they haven't processed the amount because they think it's a fraud account. Because the first transaction went through, Sirosh authorised the second one, but quickly became suspicious and tried to meet his scammer in person. I just casually asked him his address and because it was a Sydney number, he said George Street. I said okay, I said look I'm here, I would like to meet you and of course he said don't worry, don't worry, I will email you the address and I waited for half an hour and I didn't get the address so I knew I was duped. Sirosh immediately contacted police and both banks to try and put a stop to the payment on the same day, but it still went through. Sirosh, Michelle and Jodie all tricked by cunning fraudsters targeting investors. This mock-up is based off the scam websites and Cybercrime Squad commander Matt Craft has some tips on how to spot a fake. Let's start with the URL. Obviously, a normal company their URL would be www.companyname.com, usually .au in Australia. So with the URL, what we see there is changes in letters. Where you would use a K instead of a c, you would use hyphens, perhaps full stops. They can't use the legitimate URL of that company so they have to get something that is close to it. Next tip is to closely examine the contact page. What is the red flag about a proton mail email address? With that particular service there, it's often encrypted and it's an anonymous way to communicate. So once again, a legitimate business just won't be using that. How about a 1800 number, what does that tell you? 1800 numbers once again whilst they have a legitimate use, they are associated with fraud. If there is no address on the contact page of the potential investment you're looking at, what would you recommend people do? You need to know who you're dealing with, so you shouldn't be sending money to somebody that you don't know and that you cannot identify. Chris Sacchi from Australian Bond Exchange says The reality is, they pay about half to 1% per annum. Most of the scam is offering you 5%, 5.5%. So straightaway, if it's anything more than one, it's a red flag, and you need to stop. Is it too good to be true? It's a really good litmus test for identifying these types of scams. These victims have so far failed to get their money back, police are pleading with everyone to be suspicious. Investment scams are the number one way that Australians are losing money in terms of scams. What is the resounding message here when you do go onto these websites and you are considering investing hundreds of thousands of dollars? Whilst the internet, in this case this case here can work against you, the other point being is that it can also be a valuable resource for you. So when scams are identified quite quickly there's government websites that identify it and call it out. And in case you missed the names of those two websites to avoid, they are EQR Securities and Savings Connection That information is also on our website

textual.limitations: The records do not independently establish the companies' status, the websites' operation, the transactions, or the reported losses; ASR may contain transcription errors.

visual_context_notes.observation: The footage carries “A Current Affair” television branding and includes studio presentation and interview-style shots.
The email is presented alongside footage of people viewing documents and computer screens, consistent with a reported case or investigation context.

annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because it is a Current Affair report about people deceived by purported bond-investment schemes and includes interviews with victims and a cybercrime commander explaining warning signs. It describes the victims' transfers as losses and advises viewers not to send money to people they cannot identify; it does not solicit an investment or direct viewers to transfer money or provide data.
annotation.fine_grained_rationale: The video's main content examines reported fake bond investments, affected investors and warning signs; the depicted investment approaches are subjects of the report, not offers endorsed by the presenter.
